## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of the book of Isaiah

  Book title (1:1)
  1. Oracles About Judah (1:2–12:6)
  2. Oracles against the Nations (13:1–23:18)
  3. Oracles of Cosmic Judgment (24:1–27:13)
  4. Oracles Against Judah for Depending on Egypt (28:1–33:24)
  5. Oracles of Cosmic Judgment (34:1–35:10)
  6. Narrative of the Assyrian Invasion of Judah (36:1–39:8)
  7. Announcement of the End of the Babylonian Exile (40:1–55:13)
  8. The Situation in Judea After the Exile (56:1–66:24)

### What is the book of Isaiah about?

The prophecies in the book of Isaiah address two great moments of decision that the people of Judah faced 150 years apart. These were caused by the two foreign empires, Assyria and Babylon, that successively dominated this part of the world.

The first decision was whether to become a vassal state of Assyria, depend on foreign alliances for protection from Assyria, or trust in Yahweh for protection. Tiglath Pileser, who reigned from 745–727 B.C., revived the Assyrian Empire after a period of decline. Kingdoms in the western part of its former territory formed a coalition to oppose his resurgent empire. This coalition was led by King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel. At times, it included other kingdoms such as Philistia, Moab, and Edom. Rezin and Pekah invaded Judah in an attempt to replace King Ahaz, who favored Assyria, with a puppet king who would support their coalition. This threatened to end the dynasty of David. Ahaz wanted to appeal to Assyria for help, but Isaiah warned him that by cultivating that empire, he was only courting trouble. The Assyrians defeated the coalition and reasserted their control over the area. However, when one of their subsequent kings, Sargon, was killed in battle in 705 B.C., western kingdoms once again saw an opportunity to revolt. These included Judah, which was now ruled by Hezekiah, the son of Ahaz. While Hezekiah wanted to rely on Yahweh, many Judeans felt they could rely on Egypt instead to protect them against Assyria. Sargon’s son Sennacherib led a huge army to reconquer the western territory. He defeated the Egyptians and then began subjugating the smaller kingdoms that had revolted. He captured most of the fortified cities in Judah and besieged Jerusalem.

Most of the prophetic oracles in chapters 1–23 and 28–33 of the book of Isaiah relate either to the invasion of Judah by Israel and Aram or to the later invasion by Assyria. Some relate to what would happen to other kingdoms, and one (13:1–14:27) anticipates the second and later moment of decision. Chapters 36–39 are a historical narrative about the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem and its aftermath. (The same narrative is in 2 Kings 18:13–20:19.) While chapters 24–27 speak from a cosmic perspective and do not refer to specific kingdoms, it is possible that they describe the aftermath of the Assyrian invasion and siege.

The second moment of decision occurred about 150 years later. During the intervening time, the Babylonians defeated the Assyrians and replaced them as the dominant empire in this part of the world. When the Judeans revolted against them, once again misguidedly depending on Egypt, the Babylonians invaded their land, conquered and destroyed Jerusalem, and brought many of the Judeans into exile in Babylon. For seventy years, the Judeans lived as captives in that foreign land. But by around 540 B.C., the Persians, after a series of brilliant conquests under their king Cyrus, were threatening to conquer Babylon itself. The oracles in chapters 40–55 declare that Cyrus will in fact defeat the Babylonians and allow the Judeans to return home. While the oracles in chapters 34–35 also have a cosmic perspective and speak only fleetingly of specific kingdoms, it is possible that they also declare the return of the Judean exiles.

This declaration actually presented Judeans with a difficult decision. For many of them, Babylon was the only home they had ever known. It would be a long and dangerous journey back to their traditional homeland. While some of them had remained loyal to their ancestral faith in Yahweh, many others had abandoned it. They were effectively being challenged to uproot their lives and journey to resettle in a place they had either never seen or had not seen in decades. This would require them to trust in Yahweh in ways they had never done before. They had to believe that he was greater and more powerful than the gods of other nations, as these oracles insist he is.

The rest of the book of Isaiah, chapters 56–66, speaks to a situation some years after the one that chapters 40–55 address. The Persian emperor Cyrus had conquered Babylon and allowed the Jewish exiles to return home and start rebuilding Jerusalem. However, much still needed to happen within the community of returned exiles before it could become a witness to all nations of Yahweh’s glory and love, as the prophet said it was supposed to. The people were falling back into the same sins of idolatry, oppression, and injustice that had led Yahweh to take them away from the land in the first place. Some were worshiping him once again, but only through outward forms, not from the depths of their hearts. And so a further prophetic word is spoken in these chapters that calls the people who have returned to their land to return wholeheartedly to their covenant relationship with Yahweh.

While the book of Isaiah spans centuries and addresses shifting global powers, its message remains remarkably consistent: the sovereignty of Yahweh over history. Whether facing the immediate threat of Assyrian siege or the long-term displacement of Babylonian exile, the people of Judah are repeatedly called to look past the greatness of earthly empires and trust in Yahweh their God. Isaiah’s vision moves from judgment to consolation and the promise of a new thing God is doing in the world. Ultimately, the book is not just a record of two great historical moments of decision, but a single, grand narrative of a God who uses the upheavals of history to refine his people and prepare a way for all nations to behold his glory.

### Who wrote the book of Isaiah?

In three places (1:1, 2:1, and 13:1), the book attributes its prophecies to Isaiah, the son of Amoz. According to the book’s title, he prophesied during the reigns of the Judean kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. This means that he prophesied actively from about 750–700 B.C. The book does not provide many details about who this man was, but it does give a few indications. He seems to have had access to the kings of Judah and to have been aware of developments in foreign countries. It is also clear that he was well-educated and literate. These things lead many scholars to believe that he was a member of the royal court, a relative of the kings of Judah, although neither he nor any of his descendants was in line to become king. (A Jewish tradition says that his father Amoz was a brother of King Amaziah, which would have made him a first cousin to King Uzziah.) Chapters 7 and 8 indicate that Isaiah was married and had at least two sons. When he refers to his wife in chapter 8, he does not give her name, but he calls her “the prophetess.” This suggests that his wife also had a prophetic ministry. Chapter 6 relates the experience in which Yahweh called Isaiah personally to be his prophet and Isaiah willingly agreed.

From the perspective of some interpreters, the prophet who speaks in the parts of the book that relate to the end of Babylonian exile is interacting personally with the people he is addressing. This leads these interpreters to conclude that someone other than Isaiah son of Amoz, who lived 150 years earlier, spoke these oracles. They posit that Isaiah’s disciples composed them later, using the same kind of language and imagery that he did, and that they added them to an existing collection of his prophecies. These scholars view the book as analogous to a cathedral that was started by one master architect and finished by his apprentices according to his original vision. (This would be similar to the way that disciples of the apostle John seem to have added a final chapter to his gospel after his death.) For different reasons, such as, for example, the way New Testament authors attribute quotations from the earlier and later parts of the book to “Isaiah,” other interpreters believe that Isaiah son of Amoz spoke all of the words in the book that bears his name. Both of these positions about the authorship of the book are held by scholars who are equally committed to the inspiration and authority of the Bible as the word of God. Both groups of scholars believe in God’s ability to reveal future events to his prophets. It is not necessary to decide between these positions in order to translate the book. These notes will conventionally use the name Isaiah throughout to mean the author or authors of the book of Isaiah.

### What title should translators use for this book?

Translators can use a traditional title such as “The Book of Isaiah” or just “Isaiah.” They might also call it “The Sayings of Isaiah” or “The Prophecies of Isaiah.”

### What kind of writing is the book of Isaiah?

While the book of Isaiah contains some narrative passages that give details of historical developments and of Isaiah’s life, the book consists mostly of prophetic oracles. These are messages that God spoke to the people of Judah and other kingdoms through Isaiah. They are usually in the form of poetry. Many prophets in Israel used poetry when they spoke important messages that they wanted people to remember. There are some indications in the book that these poems were set to music and sung as songs. This would have given them greater impact and made them even more memorable.

Isaiah’s oracles are often based on extended images. They often move from a symbolic
depiction in the natural world to the actual situation in the human world. For example, Isaiah says in 1:8, “And the daughter of Zion is left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber field, like a besieged city.” To give another example, Isaiah uses the images of a stream and a river to describe how the Assyrians would overwhelm the land (“the waters of the River, mighty and many” will “sweep into Judah,” 8:7–8). These images sometimes develop in surprising ways. Isaiah also describes the Assyrians as a swarm of bees (7:18), but the people of Judah are then depicted as eating honey (8:22).

Prophetic oracles may also use wordplay to bring their point home, such as by using words together that have very similar sounds. For example, Isaiah says in 5:7, “he waited for justice, but behold, bloodshed.” The words translated as “justice” and “bloodshed” differ only in their last letter in Hebrew. (Notes will indicate when such wordplays are present in the text.)

Finally, some oracles are based on the repetition of an idea rather than the development of an image. They are litanies, that is, a repetitive series of phrases that serve to characterize their message as comprehensive. For example, there is a series of ten such phrases in 2:12–16. See the further discussion in Part 3.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What did Isaiah prophesy about the future Messiah of Israel?

Jews and Christians have interpreted many passages in Isaiah to be about the Messiah. In 9:1–7, Isaiah described a child being born who would rule over David’s kingdom. In chapter 11, Isaiah described a descendant of David who would have God’s spirit upon him. Several prophecies in chapters 40–66 are about “the servant.” This servant will comfort the people, rule righteously, and suffer so that God will forgive the people for sinning against him. The New Testament writers interpret these prophecies to be about Jesus Christ, the coming Messiah.

## Part 3: Translation Issues in This Book

### Parallelism

Isaiah often uses two consecutive phrases or sentences that mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it might be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. It may be clearer in your language to connect the phrases with a word other than “and” in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Another approach would be to combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way, as the UST often does. You may find that one approach works well in certain contexts and the other approach works well in other contexts. Decide as a team on a general approach to translating these parallel phrases in the book.

### Litanies

A litany is a figure of speech in which the various components of a thing are listed in a series of very similar statements. The speaker does this to indicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and without exceptions. Isaiah regularly presents litanies within his oracles. The ULT formats these as poetry or in paragraph form. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could format them as lists. For example, you could format the litany in 2:12–16 in this way:

For a day is to Yahweh of armies
against all of the proud and the ones being high
and against all of the ones being lifted up—and he will become low—
and against all the cedars of Lebanon, being high and being lifted up,
and against all of the oaks of Bashan,
and against all of the mountains being high,
and against all of the hills being lifted up,
and against every high tower,
and against every fortified wall,
and against all of the ships of Tarshish,
and against all of the boats of delight.

### Repeated images

thorn and briar

blind and deaf

highway

Jerusalem/Zion as mother

### “shall”

The ULT represents the Hebrew instructional verb form with the English  helping verb “shall.” For example, Isaiah says in 3:6 that Israelites will say to a family member, “you shall be ruler over us.” They will be instructing that family member how to act. Other ways to say this are “you are to be the ruler over us,” “you should be the ruler over us,” “we want you to be the ruler over us,” or “be the ruler over us.” Translate this form with the most  natural way in your language for giving instructions.

### “let” and “may”

The ULT uses the English helping verbs “let” and “may” to show that a speaker is expressing a desire that something happen or that someone do something. It uses the verb “let” for more assertive expressions, and it uses the verb “may” for more deferential expressions. For example, when the people say in 5:19, “let him hasten his work,” they mean, “we want him to hasten his work.” Languages that do not have a volitional form might say “he ought to hasten his work.” When Isaiah says to King Ahaz, on Yahweh’s instructions, “May you not fear,” he is being more deferential, even though the situation is urgent, because he is addressing a superior. Languages that  do not have a volitional form might say “I desire that you not fear,” or they might use an imperative with an indication that it  is a polite request, “please do not fear.” Translate this  volitional form in the most natural way in your language to indicate  that the speaker is expressing what he wants someone to do or what he  wishes someone would do.

### “saying”

The author frequently uses the term “saying” to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-quotations]])

# Introduction to Part One of the Book of Isaiah\n\nAll of the oracles collected in chapters 1–12 of the book of Isaiah relate to the moment of decision that the Judeans faced as the Assyrian empire encroached on the kingdoms to its west. (See the introduction to the book of Isaiah.) However, these oracles are not in chronological order. Many of them come from a time when the nation was being devastated by invaders, but these could come either from the reign of Ahaz, when Aram and Israel invaded Judah, or from the reign of Hezekiah, when the Assyrians invaded the land. These oracles are sequenced instead on the basis of similarities in their language, themes, and imagery. This collection begins with two series of six oracles, in 1:1–2:5 and 2:6–4:5. In each series, the first five oracles speak of Yahweh’s judgment against the Judeans, while the sixth oracle presents a hopeful picture of the future. To highlight its special character, the sixth oracle in the first series has a special heading referring again to Isaiah. It was a popular device of Hebrew literature to create a list or group of six things and then increase the total to seven. (For example, Proverbs 6:16 says that there are six things that Yahweh hates, but then increases that number to seven.) So readers of the book would have been expecting a seventh oracle after the first series, and their expectation would have been heightened when a second series of six oracles followed instead. This calls great attention to the oracle in 5:1–7, the “Song of the Vineyard,” which serves as a seventh and concluding oracle for both series. In it, Yahweh demonstrates clearly that he has given the Judeans every chance to repent and obey him, but they have not, so now they deserve judgment and punishment.

# Introduction to Isaiah 1

## Structure and Formatting

Chapter 1 of the book of Isaiah presents the first five oracles in the first series of oracles against the Judeans.

  1. Book title (1)
  2. Five oracles in the first series of six oracles about Judah
    1. The Judeans are like an animal that does not know its owner (2–3)
    2. The Judeans are like someone beaten all over his body (4–9)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Words, phrases, and images that connect oracles

One organizing principle of the oracles in this book is that an oracle that ends with a certain image will often be followed by an oracle that begins with the same image. For example, the oracle in 1:4–9 ends with a comparison to the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the oracle in 1:10–17 begins with the same comparison. Near the end of that oracle, Yahweh tells the Judeans that their hands are full of blood, and the image of red color also occurs near the start of the following oracle, when Yahweh tells them that though their sins may be like scarlet or crimson, they will become white like snow or wool. Try to translate these oracles in such a way that these connections will be clear.

# Introduction to Isaiah 2

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins with the sixth and last oracle in the first series of oracles about Judah. It is a positive oracle about future restoration. The chapter then presents the first two oracles in the second series of oracles about Judah. These are oracles that describe impending judgment. The transition into the second series can feel abrupt after the positive oracle. You may be able to signal that a new series is beginning at 2:6 by using white space or some other indicator in your translation before that verse.

  1. The last oracle in the first series of six oracles about Judah

    1. People from many nations will come to Yahweh’s temple (1–5)

  2. The first two oracles in the second series of six oracles about Judah

    1. Yahweh will punish the Judeans for idol worship (6–11)

    2. Yahweh will humble proud people, and they will flee from his wrath (12–22)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Words, phrases, and images that connect oracles

Like the oracles in chapter 1, the oracles in this chapter are connected by similarities between the end of one oracle and the start of the following one. For example, the oracle in 2:6–11 ends with synonyms that refer literally to being elevated but that mean “proud.” The following oracle, in 2:12–22, begins with similar words. Try to translate these oracles in such a way that these connections will be clear.

### Litany

In 2:12–16, Isaiah presents a litany, a list of the various components of a thing in a series of very similar statements. See the discussion of litanies in the introduction to Isaiah to decide how you will present this litany in your translation.

# Introduction to Isaiah 3

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the third, fourth, and fifth oracles in the second series of oracles about Judah. (The fifth oracle extends into the first verse of chapter 4.)

  1. The next three oracles in the second series of six oracles about Judah

    1. Judah will lose its leaders (1–7)

    2. Yahweh will judge people for what they have done (8–15)

    3. Judgment against the women of Judah (16–26)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Litanies

In 3:1–3 and 3:18–24, Isaiah presents litanies, lists of the various components of a thing in series of very similar statements. See the discussion of litanies in the introduction to Isaiah to decide how you will present these litanies in your translation.

### Wordplay[JB1.1]

As the Hebrew prophets did on many occasions, in this chapter Isaiah emphasizes a point by using words together that have very similar sounds. The words translated as “supply” and “support” in verse 1 differ in just one letter. It is often difficult to reproduce this kind of wordplay in another language, but if your language does have similar terms that you can use in this instance, as the ULT does, it would be appropriate to do that in your translation. If not, you could show the emphasis in another way, such as by saying “all support.”

# Introduction to Isaiah 5

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins with the seventh and concluding oracle in the second series of oracles about Judah. This oracle also effectively concludes the first series of six oracles. (See the introduction to Chapter 1.) After this, two new series of oracles begin. They are both interrupted by the material in 6:1–9:7, and they both conclude after that material. The first of these speaks seven woes (six in 5:8–23 and the last in 10:1–4) against the Judeans for the way they have been living. The next series describes what Yahweh has been doing to punish the Judeans and warns repeatedly that even so, “his nose [anger] has not turned back, and his hand is stretched out still.” In other words, further punishments are coming. The second oracle in this series states specifically that these will take the form of enemy armies invading the land. This is the first specific mention in the book of foreign invaders, and it provides a transition to the material in 6:1–9:7, which deals with the invasion of Judah by Aram and Israel. (See the discussion of that invasion in the introduction to Isaiah.)

  1. Seventh oracle in the second series of six oracles about Judah
    1. The Song of the Vineyard (5:1–7)
  2. First six oracles in the series of seven woes against Judah
    1. Woe to you who add house to house (8–10)
    2. Woe to those who rise early … to run after drinks (11–17)
    3. Woe to the ones dragging iniquity with cords of falsehood (18–19)
    4. Woe to those who call evil good (20)
    5. Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes (21)
    6. Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine (22–23)
3. First two oracles in the series about present and impending punishments
    1. Yahweh will punish the people like a devouring flame (24–25)
    2. A powerful foreign army will invade Judah (26–30)

### Wordplay[JB3.1]

As the Hebrew prophets did on many occasions, in this chapter Isaiah emphasizes a point by using words together that have very similar sounds. In verse 7, he says, “he waited for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, a cry.” The words translated as “justice” and “bloodshed” differ only in their last letter in Hebrew. Similarly, the words for “righteousness” and a “cry” differ in only one letter. It is often difficult to reproduce this kind of wordplay in another language, but if your language does have similar terms that you can use in these instances, it would be appropriate to do that in your translation. If not, you could show the emphasis in another way, such as by saying “only bloodshed” and “nothing but a cry.”

# Introduction to Isaiah 6

## Structure and Formatting

In chapters 6–8 of the book of Isaiah, there is a break in the oracles about Judah that make up the rest of chapters 1–13. During this break, the book presents narratives about Isaiah himself. They describe how Yahweh called Isaiah to be a prophet and some of the first things Yahweh sent him to tell the kings and people of Judah. These narratives describe the earliest events that the book of Isaiah records. Writers in many cultures would relate the earliest events in a story first, but there are reasons why these narratives about Isaiah are not placed first in the book. For one thing, Hebrew writers often put their most important material not at the beginning or end of a work but in the middle. That was their way of showing its importance. Also, the book of Isaiah is not a biography of the prophet, and the collection of his oracles is not designed to show who he was. Instead, it presents a case on behalf of Yahweh that the people of Judah and Israel had been very unfaithful to their covenant with him, and so it was appropriate for him to judge and punish them in order to correct them. So the book begins by calling on the heavens and the earth as witnesses to the covenant and by summarizing the charges against the people (1:2). It only introduces Isaiah after presenting much evidence to support those charges. The presentation of evidence continues in chapter 9, after this section that tells about Isaiah personally. This section has these parts:

  1. Narratives about Isaiah

    1. The calling of Isaiah (6:1–13)

    2. A sign for Ahaz: a child will be born (7:1–24)

    3. Isaiah and his children (8:1–18)

    4. The child will bring light where there was darkness (8:19–9:7)

As the outline shows, this chapter describes how Yahweh called Isaiah to be a prophet.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Descriptive term for the woman who is going to have a son

In verse 14, Isaiah tells King Ahaz that Yahweh is going to give him a sign. As he speaks of a woman who is going to have a son, Isaiah uses a term from his culture that describes a young woman of marriageable age. It could describe a woman who was not yet married or a woman who was married but had not yet had children. Interpreters believe that in context, Isaiah is referring either to the primary wife of King Ahaz, whose first son would become the next king and continue the dynasty of David, or to his own wife, whom he describes in the next chapter. Either way, the original point of the sign was that before this boy was old enough to know right from wrong, the countries whose kings were invading Judah would be destroyed. The boy’s name, Immanuel, which means “God with us,” was a further guarantee from Yahweh that he would help the Judeans. However, in the New Testament, we learn that there was a deeper fulfillment of the sign that Isaiah described. Matthew relates in his gospel how Mary conceived Jesus while she was still a virgin and how Jesus literally was “God with us.” So that your readers can appreciate this connection, if at all possible, use a term in your translation here that could describe either a young wife who had not yet had children or an unmarried woman who had never had sexual relations. The ULT does that by using the term “maiden.”

# Introduction to Isaiah 9

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, verses 1–7 are the continuation of the oracle that begins at 8:19, which describes how the child whose birth was announced in chapter 7 will strengthen and protect the kingdom of Judah. (Many interpreters understand this oracle to apply initially to Hezekiah, the son of Ahaz, who was a godly king. It has a further fulfillment in the ministry of Jesus, as Matthew 4:12–16 indicates.)

The rest of this chapter, verses 8–21, is a resumption of the oracle that begins in 5:24–25, in which Yahweh describes the consequences of the people’s unfaithfulness and disobedience. This oracle has a refrain, “In all of this, his nose [anger] has not turned back, and his hand is still stretched out,” which occurs in 5:25 and then in verses 12, 17, and 21 of this chapter. In other words, the central section of narratives about Isaiah ends at 9:7. The oracles about Judah, which were interrupted at 6:1, resume at 9:8.

  1. Narratives about Isaiah (conclusion)

    1. The child will bring light where there was darkness (1–7, continued from chapter 8)

# Introduction to Isaiah 10

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, verses 1–4 are the continuation of the Woe Oracle that began in 5:8–25. There were six woes there, creating the expectation that a seventh woe would eventually be pronounced, and that happens in verses 1–4. So the overall structure of 5:8–10:4 is:

 Woe Oracle (5:8–25)

 Consequence Oracle (5:24–30)

 Narratives about Isaiah (6:1–9:7)

 Consequence Oracle, concluded (9:8–21)

 Woe Oracle, concluded (10:1–4)

The first and last parts match, and the second and fourth parts match, enclosing the middle part. Hebrew writers considered this kind of arrangement elegant. (It is known as a “chiasm.”) To show that the conclusion of the Woe Oracle here also concludes this entire arrangement, the refrain of the Consequence Oracle, “In all of this, his nose has not turned back, and his hand is still stretched out,” also occurs at the end of the seventh woe in 10:4. Represent this language consistently in your translation.

Verses 5–34 of this chapter present a further woe, but it should not be understood as an eighth woe in the series that leads up to it. Instead, it is a brief change of focus away from the Judeans to a foreign nation, Assyria. (This anticipates the collection of oracles against the nations in Part Two of the book, in chapters 13–23.) Assyria has been in the background all along as a threatening foreign power that Yahweh will use to punish and correct the Judeans. Now it comes to the foreground as Yahweh declares that it has become too proud and unrestrained, thinking that by its own power and wisdom it has conquered other nations, and so he will destroy it. This oracle is spoken from the vantage point of a time farther in the future than the other oracles in Part One. It has three parts:

  1. Rebuke of the Assyrians for their pride (5–19)

  2. Promise that a remnant of Israelites will survive and be restored (20–27)

  3. The Assyrian army’s advance toward Jerusalem, ending in its destruction (28–34)

# Introduction to Isaiah 11

## Structure and Formatting

Many of the books in the Bible that are collections of prophetic oracles follow a certain pattern. They first present oracles of judgment against God’s people, then oracles of judgment against other nations, and then oracles that promise restoration to God’s people. The oracles in Part One of the book of Isaiah (chapters 1–12) follow this pattern:

  1. Oracles of judgment against the Judeans (chapters 1–9)

  2. An oracle of judgment against the Assyrians (chapter 10)

  3. Oracles of restoration for the Judeans (chapters 11–12)

(There is also a hopeful oracle within the central section of narratives about Isaiah, in 8:19–9:7)

The oracle in chapter 11 has two parts:

  1. A descendant of Jesse will become a godly king (1–10)

  2. Yahweh will regather his scattered people into a united, powerful nation (11–16)

#Introduction to Part Two of the Book of Isaiah

Part Two of the book of Isaiah (chapters 13–23) presents oracles against other nations:

  1. Babylon (13:1–14:23)
  2. Assyria (14:24–27)
  3. The Philistines (14:28–32)
  4. Moab (15:1–16:14)
  5. Aram and Israel (17:1–14)
  6. Cush (the Upper Nile region) (18:1–7)
  7. Egypt (19:1–24)
  8. Egypt and Cush (20:1–6)
  9. Babylon (21:1–10)
  10. Edom (21:11–12)
  11. Arabia (21:13–17)
  12. Judah and Jerusalem (22:1–25)
  13. Tyre (23:1–18)

The first oracle is against Babylon, even though the Babylonians conquered and destroyed Jerusalem more than a hundred years after the Assyrians besieged that city. See the discussion in the introduction to Isaiah of how the book addresses two great moments of decision that the people of Judah faced 150 years apart that were caused by the foreign empires that successively dominated their part of the world, Assyria and Babylon. The oracle against Babylon may have been placed first in the final arrangement of the book of Isaiah because the return from Babylonian exile after the destruction of that empire was the historical event that was most vivid for readers of the book.

# Introduction to Isaiah 14

## Structure and Formatting

The oracle against Babylon that began in 13:1 continues through 14:23. This chapter then presents oracles against Assyria and Philistia.

  1. Oracle against Babylon (1–23)

    1. Yahweh will restore the Israelites (1–2)

    2. A taunt-song that the Israelites will sing against the Babylonians (3–11)

    3. The defeat and disgrace of the king of Babylon (12–23)

  2. Oracle against Assyria (24–27)

  3. Oracle against Philistia (28–32)

# Introduction to Isaiah 18

## Structure and Formatting

By the time the Assyrian Empire was encroaching on the kingdoms to its west, rulers from the region south of Egypt, known as Cush or Nubia, had reunited the fragmented Egyptian kingdom under their rule. The oracle in chapter 18 describes their land as “along the rivers of Cush” (the upper branches of the Nile) and refers to it as “the land of whirring of wings” because of the loud insects that lived by those rivers. It identifies these rulers by their height and smooth skin. The oracle indicates that they had sent messengers to try to persuade the Judeans to join them in an alliance against Assyria. But in response, Isaiah sends the messengers back home, telling them that Yahweh has said that he will deal with the Assyrian threat himself, suddenly and powerfully.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

Many phrases from verse 2 are repeated in verse 7. This gives the oracle a clear beginning and ending. It also reflects the progression from the Egyptians sending messengers to Judah as a potential client state to the Egyptians sending tribute to Yahweh to acknowledge him as the one true God. # Introduction to Isaiah 19

## Structure and Formatting

Like the oracle in the previous chapter, the oracle in Isaiah 19 is about Egypt. However, it comes from an earlier time. It describes the civil strife and lack of wise counsel that allowed a “fierce king,” a Nubian ruler, to take control of the land. It uses the drying up of the Nile River as an image to represent the economic and social decline of Egypt during this period. But at the end, the oracle looks forward to a future time when the Egyptians will worship Yahweh. They and the people of another great empire that oppressed the Israelites, Assyria, will be at peace with Israel and respect their spiritual leadership.

  1. Civil strife in Egypt permits a “fierce king” to take control (1–4)
  2. A description of the Nile River drying up (5–10)
  3. The lack of wise counsel in Egypt (11–15)
  4. A future vision of peace between Egypt, Israel, and Assyria (16–25)

# Introduction to Isaiah 20

## Structure and Formatting

The oracle in chapter 20 is about Egypt and Cush, like the oracles in the two preceding chapters. It is different from those oracles in that it does not present a poem (probably the words to a song). Instead, it describes how Yahweh told Isaiah to act out a prophetic sign on a certain occasion, and it then explains the meaning of the sign. Although people in the smaller kingdoms west of Assyria, including many in Judah, wanted to rely on Egypt for protection, the Assyrians would conquer Egypt and take its people captive. The implication, which many other oracles in Isaiah bring out (especially in Part Four), is that the Judeans should rely on Yahweh instead.

# Introduction to Isaiah 21

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents three further oracles against the nations. The first oracle is about how the Medes and Elamites will conquer and destroy Babylon. It comes from the later time period that the book of Isaiah addresses, the same period as in the oracle in chapters 13 and 14 and in Part Seven, chapters 40–55.

The second oracle is about Edom, a kingdom to the south of Judah. Isaiah makes a wordplay on its name, rearranging the consonants and calling it Dumah, since that means “silence.” (There was a city in the eastern desert called Dumah, but this oracle is not about that city.) This oracle is apparently a response to an inquiry from the Edomites about whether their domination by Assyria is about to end. The answer is that it is about to end, but the Edomites will only have a short respite before they are conquered again. That will happen when the Babylonians displace the Assyrians as the dominant power in the region.

The third oracle is about the powerful Arabian tribes that conducted caravans through the desert for trade. It predicts that they will no longer control their area, and they will have to leave their established routes and hide where they can, because enemy soldiers will invade the area. It is probably referring to the Assyrians, who expanded into that area to get control of the trade routes.

  1. Babylon (1–10)
  2. Dumah (Edom) (11–12)
  3. Arabia (13–17)

# Introduction to Isaiah 22

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents a pair of oracles that address the situation in Jerusalem during the Assyrian siege of 701 B.C. (That is described in chapters 36 and 37.) In the first oracle, Yahweh chastises the Judeans for their response to the siege. It describes how the Assyrians surrounded the city and what preparations the Judeans made to resist them. But it then describes how, instead of repenting sorrowfully and sincerely, many Judeans held feasts to have a good time before they died. In the second oracle, Yahweh chastises Shebna, the official in charge of the royal palace, for having a splendid tomb carved out for himself on a cliff overlooking the city. He too, instead of sincerely asking Yahweh for help, only wanted to die in style. Yahweh says that he will replace Shebna with a godly man, Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah. (Readers learn in chapters 36 and 37 that Eliakim was one of the royal officials who engaged the Assyrian officers and then went to Isaiah to ask him to pray for the people of Jerusalem.)

  1. The people of Jerusalem celebrate fatalistically rather than repent (1–14)
  2. Yahweh will replace Shebna with Eliakim (15–25)

# Introduction to Isaiah 23

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents an oracle about the city of Tyre. It was a great trading port and fortress city on an island just off the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea. Ships that sailed to ports all around that sea loaded and unloaded goods there. The people of Tyre became wealthy particularly by importing and exporting grain that was grown in Egypt. The oracle warns that the city will be destroyed and its trade will be ruined. Because it draws a comparison to the way the Assyrians destroyed Babylon (their emperor Sennacherib did that in 689 B.C.), it seems to come from the period of Assyrian ascendancy. The Assyrians did not completely destroy Tyre, but they did reduce it to a vassal state and take much of its revenue in taxes and tribute. The oracle had a further fulfillment when the Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city for 13 years. The total ruin that this oracle predicts occurred in 332 B.C. when Alexander the Great captured and destroyed the city by building a land bridge out to the island. The oracle ends on a hopeful note, however. Looking to the future[JB6.1], it predicts that Tyre will become prosperous again, and instead of hoarding its wealth, it will devote it to Yahweh’s temple and the support of his people. This is like the vision of future peace in 19:16–25.

  1. Tyre will be ruined (1–14)

  2. Tyre will be restored (15–18)

# Introduction to Part Three of the Book of Isaiah

The oracles in Part Three of the book of Isaiah (chapters 24–27) describe actions by Yahweh that are worldwide in scope, affecting even the created order. These oracles apply on a cosmic scale the themes of both judgment and restoration that characterize the prophecies against the nations in Part Two. As a result, it is difficult to determine what specific historical situation inspired the oracles in this part of the book.

The oracles in chapters 24 and 25 announce and celebrate the destruction of a great city. Some interpreters identify this city as Babylon and conclude that these two oracles come from the time of the second great moment of decision that the book of Isaiah addresses, when God’s people were called to return from exile in Babylon to the land of Israel. (See the discussion in the introduction to the book of Isaiah.) That is possible; however, these oracles also look forward to the time when God will judge the entire world, so their application is not limited to a single historical situation.

The oracles in chapters 25 and 27 have some themes in common with the ones in chapters 11 and 12, at the end of Part One. They express the hope that God’s anger will shortly pass and that all nations will learn about God from what he does for his people. A passage in the last oracle in this section, 27:2–5, echoes and reverses the song of the vineyard in 5:1–7. The vision of restoration in these oracles could come originally from the time of the first great moment of decision, the Assyrian crisis. But their application should also not be limited to a single situation. The oracles in all of Part Three seem to have been shaped and collected to present a worldwide vision of what Yahweh will ultimately do to make all nations recognize that he is the one true God.

1. A vision of the cosmic destruction of Yahweh’s enemies (24:1–23)
2. Yahweh destroys an oppressive city, makes a feast, and punishes Moab (25:1–12)
3. Wait patiently for Yahweh to punish wicked people and rescue righteous people (26:1–21)
4. Yahweh will destroy his enemies and regather and restore his own people (27:1–13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why does this universal oracle single out Moab at the end?

As the introduction to Part Three of Isaiah explains, the oracles in chapters 24–27 have a universal scope. Their meaning seems to transcend any one specific historical situation. Nevertheless, in verses 10–12, this oracle describes judgment against a particular nation, Moab. Many interpreters believe that Moab is being used here as a specific example of a general truth. Moab, which was a longtime enemy of Israel, may be used as an illustration of what will happen to all nations that proudly oppose Yahweh and his purposes for the world.

# Introduction to Isaiah 27

## Structure and Formatting

  1. Yahweh will defeat Leviathan, cosmic chaos (1)
  2. Yahweh will restore Israel (2–6)
  3. Yahweh limited Israel’s punishment (7–9)
  4. Yahweh completely destroys cities that never repent (10–11)
  5. Yahweh will regather the Israelites (12–13)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

In 5:1–7, Yahweh sings a song about a vineyard that represents the people of Israel and Judah. He cultivates the vines, but they still produce wild, sour grapes. So he allows the vineyard land to become wild again. That represents how he will allow enemies to conquer the Israelites because of their disobedience. In 27:2–6, Yahweh sings another song about a vineyard. In this song, he describes how he will continually guard and protect it. This is a reversal of the earlier song. It shows that Yahweh will now regather the people from exile and restore them to their land. So that your readers can appreciate this, try to translate the terms and phrases that the songs share in the same way in both chapters. For example, 5:6 says that “briar and thorn will come up” where vines once grew. In 27:4, Yahweh says that if a “briar” or “thorn” grows in his vineyard, he will pull it up and burn it. It would be helpful to use the same terms for those plants in both places.

# Introduction to Part Four of the Book of Isaiah

Part Four of the book of Isaiah presents a series of oracles that pronounce woes against Judah for depending on Egypt for protection against Assyria. So these oracles come from the time of the first great moment of decision that the book of Isaiah addresses, the Assyrian crisis. (See the discussion in the introduction to the book of Isaiah.) There are six oracles, but the last one begins with an implied double “woe,” which poetically suggests a total of the expected seven. The overall message of this part of the book is that the Judeans are foolish and disobedient to depend on the Egyptians, mere humans, for protection. They should depend instead on Yahweh, the great and powerful God who rules the entire world.

  1. A woe against the drunken leaders of Samaria and Jerusalem (28:1–29)
  2. A woe against Jerusalem, which an enemy army will besiege (29:1–14)
  3. A woe against those who try to hide their plans from Yahweh (29:15–24)
  4. A woe against the Judeans for rebelling against Yahweh (30:1–33)
  5. A woe against the Judeans for going to Egypt for help (31:1–32:20)
  6. A woe against the Assyrians and a promise of help to Judah (33:1–24)

# Introduction to Isaiah 29

## Structure and Formatting

Isaiah 29 presents the second and third of the six woe oracles in Part Four of the book. These oracles rebuke the leaders and people of Judah for depending on Egypt instead of trusting in Yahweh for protection against Assyria. The two oracles here have these sections:

  1. Yahweh will humble Jerusalem by having an enemy army besiege it (1–14)
    1. The people of Jerusalem will be humbled even though they follow religious forms (1–4)
    2. Yahweh will ultimately defeat the besieging army (5–8)
    3. Jerusalem’s prophets are currently unable to understand what Yahweh is doing (9–14)
  2. A woe against those who try to hide their plans from Yahweh (15–24)
    1. Those who hide their plans are acting as if they are greater than Yahweh (15–16)
    2. Yahweh will act to empower weak people and humble powerful people (17–21)
    3. Yahweh will restore the Israelites and they will worship him again (22–24)

# Introduction to Isaiah 30

## Structure and Formatting

Isaiah 30 presents the fourth of the six woe oracles in Part Four of the book. These oracles rebuke the leaders and people of Judah for depending on Egypt instead of trusting in Yahweh for protection against Assyria. This fourth oracle has these sections:

  1. The Judeans will be ashamed for rebelliously sending ambassadors to Egypt (1–5)
  2. It is useless for the Judeans to send gifts dangerously through the desert to Egypt (6–7)
  3. The Judeans will suffer defeat and disaster for rebelling against Yahweh (8–17)
  4. Yahweh will graciously restore the Judeans if they return to him (18–26)
  5. Yahweh will powerfully defeat the Assyrians (27–33)

# Introduction to Isaiah 31

## Structure and Formatting

Isaiah 31 presents the first part of the fifth of the six woe oracles in Part Four of the book. These oracles rebuke the leaders and people of Judah for depending on Egypt instead of trusting in Yahweh for protection against Assyria. (The rest of this oracle is in chapter 32.) This part of the oracle has these sections:

  1. Yahweh rebukes the people for relying on Egypt (1–3)
  2. Yahweh himself will protect Jerusalem (4–5)
  3. Yahweh calls the people to repent and abandon their idols (6–7)
  4. Yahweh himself will defeat the Assyrians (8–9)

Isaiah is using the word **Woe** to express a strong feeling of warning and judgment against those who seek help from Egypt instead of from Yahweh. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How horrible it will be for]

# Isaiah 32 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Isaiah 32 contrasts present corruption with future restoration. It opens with a vision of a righteous king (vv. 1-8), warns complacent women of coming desolation (vv. 9-14), and promises renewal when Yahweh pours out his [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/spirit]] (vv. 15-20).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Righteousness and Justice in Governance

The chapter pairs [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/righteous]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]] as qualities of the promised king (v. 1) and as the fruit of the Spirit’s outpouring (vv. 16-17).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

The chapter makes extensive use of synonymous parallel lines throughout its three sections.

# Introduction to Isaiah 33

Isaiah 33 presents the last of the six woe oracles in Part Four of the book. These oracles rebuke the leaders and people of Judah for depending on Egypt instead of trusting in Yahweh for protection against Assyria. This last oracle has these sections:

  1. Yahweh will destroy Judah’s enemies and restore the people (1–6)
  2. The current desperate situation in Judah (7–9)
  3. Yahweh will come and destroy his enemies (10–13)
  4. Righteous people will be safe (14–16)

# Introduction to Part Five of the Book of Isaiah

Part Five of the book of Isaiah (chapters 34 and 35) apparently speaks to the second great moment of decision that the book of Isaiah addresses, when God’s people were called to return from exile in Babylon to the land of Israel. (See the discussion in the introduction to the book of Isaiah.)

The first oracle (in chapter 34) is spoken against Edom, one of Judah’s neighbors, which did not help the Judeans when the Babylonians conquered them. Instead, the Edomites cheered for their defeat and turned their survivors and refugees over to the Babylonians. Like the similar oracles in Jeremiah 49 and Obadiah 1, this oracle predicts that Yahweh will destroy the Edomites to punish them for this. Many interpreters believe that, as in the case of Moab in Part Three, Edom is being used here as a specific example of a general truth. Beyond the specific historical context, Edom may serve as an illustration of what will happen to all nations that Yahweh judges and punishes. In other words, like the oracles in Part Three, the oracles here look forward to the time when God will judge the entire world. They too speak in cosmic language and look to some more distant future events. So their application is not limited to a single historical situation. 

The other oracle in this short part of the book (in chapter 35) promises that Yahweh will bring the people of Judah back from exile in Babylon. It describes creation itself being transformed in the process.

  1. Yahweh will punish the Edomites for what they did to the Judeans (34:1–17)
  2. Yahweh will bring the Judeans back from exile through a transformed desert (35:1–10)

# Introduction to Part Six of the Book of Isaiah

Part Six of the book of Isaiah (chapters 36–39) describes the culmination of the Assyrian crisis. That crisis lasted for an entire generation. It provides the background for the oracles collected in Parts One and Four of the book. These chapters relate how it ended. They consist mostly of historical narratives, with some poetic oracles interspersed. That is the opposite of the materials in the other parts of the book.

Chapters 36 and 37, which describe how a huge Assyrian army invaded Judah and threatened Jerusalem, are virtually identical with 2 Kings 18:13–20:19. If you have already translated that material, this should help you translate these chapters. However, be alert to the subtle differences in the language at various places throughout the material.

Chapters 38 and 39 describe events that occurred a couple of years before the events of chapters 36 and 37. Chapter 38 describes how Hezekiah got a deadly illness, but Yahweh enabled him to recover. Chapter 39 describes how envoys then came from Babylon to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery and, implicitly, to recruit him as an ally for a coalition against Assyria. Second Kings 18:14–26 records that when the Assyrian king invaded Judah, Hezekiah sent him a huge tribute to try to keep him from attacking Jerusalem. But in chapter 39, Hezekiah’s storehouses are still full, since he shows their treasures to the Babylonian envoys. So chapters 38 and 39 are out of historical order. The book places their accounts after the account of the Assyrian invasion because the visit from the Babylonian messengers foreshadows the Babylonian captivity, which will be the setting for the oracles in Part Seven, chapters 40–55.

# Introduction to Isaiah 36

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter relates events that took place around 701 BC. Hezekiah has succeeded his father Ahaz as king of Judah. For many years, he has appeased the Assyrians by sending tribute, as his father did. But since he is a genuine believer in Yahweh, he does not want to worship the gods of the Assyrians, as his father did and as they expect him to do. So he has joined a rebellious coalition led by Egypt. The Assyrian emperor Sennacherib has responded to this coalition by leading a huge army to the region and defeating the Egyptians. He is now overrunning the kingdom of Judah, conquering its fortified cities one by one. While he is besieging the city of Lachish, he sends his commander, the Rabshakeh, to Jerusalem to demand that Hezekiah surrender.

  1. The Rabshakeh comes to Jerusalem and Hezekiah’s officials meet him (1–3)
  2. The Rabshakeh addresses Hezekiah’s officials (4–10)
  3. The Rabshakeh addresses the people of Jerusalem (11–21)
  4. Hezekiah’s officials report to him (22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did the Assyrians stop where they did?

The story says in 36:2 that the large Assyrian army that advanced against Jerusalem stopped at “the conduit of the Upper Pool on the highway of the Field of the Fuller.” One reason for stopping and apparently setting up camp there was probably the need for water for a large army. According to an account in 2 Chronicles of these same events, Hezekiah had blocked up all the water sources around the city in order to keep the Assyrians from having a water supply. But the location where their army stopped was right next to an aqueduct that brought water down to Jerusalem from springs above the city. That provided a ready source of water. This was also a prominent location right outside the city walls. This allowed the Assyrian officials to demand a conference with King Hezekiah’s representatives that would take place within the hearing of Judeans who gathered on the city walls. The Assyrians exploited this and said things publicly to try to terrify and demoralize the Judeans.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Levels of quotation

There are multiple levels of quotation in the long quotations in verses 4–10 and 13–20. In the first section, it is complicated to follow who is speaking and on whose behalf. But here is one probable explanation. This is the interpretation that the ULT follows.
- Verse 4 introduces three levels of quotation. The author begins quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1). The Rabshakeh begins to tell Hezekiah’s officials what he wants them to say to Hezekiah (level 2). This includes the beginning of a quotation from Sennacherib, the king of Assyria (level 3).
- The third-level quotation continues through verses 5 and 6. A fourth-level quotation begins in verse 5, as Sennacherib quotes something that Hezekiah is supposedly saying. The pronoun “you” is singular because Sennacherib is addressing Hezekiah. The second-level and third-level quotations that began in verse 4 conclude at the end of verse 6.
- In verse 7, there are two levels of quotation. The “you” in “if you say” is plural, so the Rabshakeh is now addressing Hezekiah’s officials directly. He speaks of Hezekiah in the third person. But he quotes what the officials might say and what Hezekiah has said.
- The first-level quotation from the Rabshakeh continues in v. 8, but now the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah directly. (He is implicitly expecting the Judean officials to pass along his words). The implied “you” in the imperative “wager” and the pronoun “yourself” are singular, but the king of Assyria is spoken of in the third person (“my master”), so the Rabshakeh is not quoting the king as he did in vv. 4–6.
- This seems to be the case in v. 9, as well, where the Rabshakeh continues to speak of Sennacherib as “my master.”
- But the speaker in v. 10 seems to be Sennacherib again, speaking of himself in the first person. (The Rabshakeh would not say of himself, “Now have I come up against this place.”) This is an implicit return to the third-level quotation, although the author does not signal it directly in the text.
Notes describe different possible ways of indicating the speakers throughout this long quotation.

The long quotation in verses 13–205 contains three levels of quotation, but the identity of the speakers seems clear throughout. Notes also describe ways of indicating the speakers throughout this quotation.

The king of Assyria is using the term **Behold** to focus Hezekiah’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Quote: בָטַ֡חְתָּ עַל־מִשְׁעֶנֶת֩ הַ⁠קָּנֶ֨ה הָ⁠רָצ֤וּץ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם
Note: The king of Assyria is speaking as if **Egypt** were actually a **broken reed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you believe that you can rely on Egypt, but that is like using a broken reed as a staff]

The king of Assyria is using the possessive form to describe a **staff** that consists of a **broken reed**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in this broken reed, Egypt, as a staff]

Quote: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵ֛י הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֥חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ
Note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form to challenge the claim that Hezekiah’s official might make that they are trusting in Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And you should not say to me, ‘We trust in Yahweh our God,’ since he is the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, ‘To the face of this altar in Jerusalem, you shall prostrate yourselves’!]

Quote: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵ֛י הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֥חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ
Note: The second-level and third-level quotations that began in verse 4 conclude at the end of verse 6. There are two levels of quotation in this verse. The Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah’s official directly (level 1), and he quotes what the official might say and what Hezekiah has said (level 2). If you have been marking levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate punctuation in your language for the levels in this verse.

Quote: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵ֛י הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֥חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that Hezekiah should not tell him that you Judeans are trusting in Yahweh your God. After all, Hezekiah himself is the one who has removed the  high places and  altars and told the people of Judah and Jerusalem that they must prostrate themselves to the face of the altar in Jerusalem.]

The word **you** is singular in the first instance because the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah’s official. The word **you** in the second instance and the word **yourselves** are plural because Hezekiah was addressing all of the Judeans. So use singular and plural forms respectively in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

By **We**, Hezekiah’s officials would mean themselves and their fellow Judeans but not the Rabshakeh, to whom they would be speaking. So use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **Judah** and **Jerusalem** represent the people who live in those places. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of Judah and Jerusalem]
This is a Hebrew idiom meaning “Before” or  “in the presence of.” Alternate translation: [In front of]

Quote: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הִתְעָ֣רֶב נָ֔א אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְ⁠אֶתְּנָ֤ה לְ⁠ךָ֙ אַלְפַּ֣יִם סוּסִ֔ים אִם־תּוּכַ֕ל לָ֥⁠תֶת לְ⁠ךָ֖ רֹכְבִ֥ים עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [And now, please invite Hezekiah to make a wager with my master, the king of Assyria. Tell him that I will give him 2,000 horses if he is able to put riders on them for himself]

This is the beginning of something that the Rabshakeh is saying directly to Hezekiah. He implicitly wants the Judean officials to quote to Hezekiah what he says. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in your translation. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah from me, ‘And now]

**And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce an important point such as the implications of what they were just saying. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation.

The implied “you” in the imperative **wager** and the pronouns **you** and **yourself** are singular in each instance because the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah directly. The words “you” and “yourself” are singular in verse 9 for the same reason. So use singular forms in these verses in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Quote: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְטַנִּ֑ים וַ⁠תִּבְטַ֤ח לְ⁠ךָ֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְ⁠רֶ֖כֶב וּ⁠לְ⁠פָרָשִֽׁים
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [But ask him how he would turn back the face of a captain of one of the least servants of my master. Tell him I know that is why he is trusting for himself in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen]

Quote: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְטַנִּ֑ים
Note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But even then, you would not be able to turn back the face of a captain of one of the least servants of my master!]

Quote: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְטַנִּ֑ים
Note: The Rabshakeh is using one part of a person, his **face**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But how would you turn back a captain of one of the least servants of my master] or [But how would you force a captain to retreat even if he was one of the least servants of my master]

The Rabshakeh is using the possessive form to describe a **captain** who would be **one of the least servants** of the king of Assyria, that is, one of his weakest soldiers. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a captain who was among the least servants of my master]

This is the end of what the Rabshakeh is saying directly to Hezekiah. In the next verse, the Rabshakeh quotes the end of the message from Sennacherib that he wants the officials to give to Hezekiah. If you have been marking levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate closing punctuation at the end of this verse.

Quote: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את לְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָ֑⁠הּ יְהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י עֲלֵ֛ה אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את וְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָֽ⁠הּ
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah that the king of Assyria says that he has not come up against this land to destroy it without Yahweh. Yahweh told him to go up against this land and destroy it]

Quote: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את לְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָ֑⁠הּ
Note: This is the beginning of something that Sennacherib is saying directly to Hezekiah. It is the rest of the message that the Rabshakeh began to quote in verses 4–6. The Rabshakeh implicitly wants the Judean officials to quote this to Hezekiah as something that Sennacherib has said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in your translation. Alternate translation: [Say to Hezekiah, ‘Thus says the great king, “And have I come up]

Quote: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את לְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָ֑⁠הּ
Note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not think that I have come up against this land to destroy it without Yahweh!]

Sennacherib is not using the phrase **without Yahweh** to mean that Hezekiah should not think that he has come without Yahweh accompanying him. Rather, he means that he has come after receiving a command from Yahweh. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [without receiving a command to do so from Yahweh]

Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah are speaking of themselves in the third person as **your servants** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to us, your servants,]

Quote: דַּבֶּר־נָ֤א אֶל־עֲבָדֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ אֲרָמִ֔ית כִּ֥י שֹׁמְעִ֖ים אֲנָ֑חְנוּ
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since we, your servants, understand Aramaic, please speak to us in that language]

Eliakim is using the name of the dialect of Hebrew, **Judean**, that people spoke in the kingdom of Judah. Some versions use the name of the language rather than the name of this dialect and say “in Hebrew.” If you have decided to use the same names in your translation that the biblical author does, you may wish to use the name, **Judean**, here. If not, you may wish to use the name “Hebrew” here.

Here, **ears** represent “hearing.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the hearing of the people who are on the wall] or [, since the people who are on the wall can hear us]

Quote: הַ⁠אֶ֨ל אֲדֹנֶ֤י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ שְׁלָחַ֣⁠נִי אֲדֹנִ֔⁠י לְ⁠דַבֵּ֖ר אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֑לֶּה הֲ⁠לֹ֣א עַל־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים הַ⁠יֹּֽשְׁבִים֙ עַל־הַ֣⁠חוֹמָ֔ה לֶ⁠אֱכֹ֣ל אֶת־חראי⁠הם וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׁתּ֛וֹת אֶת־שיני⁠הם עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם
Note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My master did not send me to speak these words only to your master and to you! He also sent me to speak them to the men sitting on the wall, who will eat their dung and drink their urine with you!]

Rabshakey is using the term **words** to represent what his **master** said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this message]

Even though the author says that the Rabshakeh spoke to **them**, the word **your** and the word **you** in its first instance are singular because the Rabshakeh is replying directly to Eliakim, who spoke on behalf of all three Judean officials. The word **you** in its second instance is plural because the Rabshakeh is including Shebnah and Joah in what he says will happen. Use the appropriate singular and plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The author probably does not mean that the Rabshakeh had been sitting down and having a private conversation with the Judean officials and that he then **stood** up. If the conversation had been private, there would have been no need for Eliakim to ask him to speak in Aramaic so that the people on the wall would not understand. So the author probably means that the Rabshakeh stood in such a way that his speech to the people on the wall would seem even more forceful and intimidating. Alternate translation: [And the Rabshakeh assumed a dominating stance]
See how you have translated the phrase **and said** elsewhere when it introduces a direct quotation.

Quote: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ אַל־יַשִּׁ֥א לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּ֥י לֹֽא־יוּכַ֖ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶֽם
Note: See the note about the multiple levels of quotation in the introduction to this chapter. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate all of this long quotation so that there are not quotations within quotations. Alternate translation: [The king says that you should not let Hezekiah deceive you, since he is not able to deliver you]

Quote: אַל־יַשִּׁ֥א לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּ֥י לֹֽא־יוּכַ֖ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶֽם
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since Hezekiah is not able to deliver you, do not let him deceive you]

The word **you** is plural in both of these instances because king of Assyria, speaking through the Rabshakeh, is addressing the Judeans who have gathered on the city wall. For the same reason, the word “you” and the implied “you” in imperatives are also plural throughout verses 15–17. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Quote: וְ⁠אַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְ⁠כֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ יְהוָ֑ה לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
Note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. The Rabshakeh is quoting the king of Assyria (level 2), also continuing from the previous verse. The king is quoting Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

Quote: וְ⁠אַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְ⁠כֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ יְהוָ֑ה לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The king says that you should not let Hezekiah make you trust in Yahweh by telling you that delivering, Yahweh will deliver all of you, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria]

According to the king of Assyria, Hezekiah has been repeating forms of the verb **deliver** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will certainly deliver us]
By **us**, Hezekiah means to include both himself and those to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction, here and in verse 32.

The expression **will not be given** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will not give this city]
Here, **hand** represents “control” or “power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the control of]

Rabshakeh is saying what he wants the people to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that you do not listen to Hezekiah] or [You should not listen to Hezekiah]

Quote: כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֗וּר עֲשֽׂוּ־אִתִּ֤⁠י בְרָכָה֙ וּ⁠צְא֣וּ אֵלַ֔⁠י וְ⁠אִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵנָת֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵי־בוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [for the king of Assyria is telling you to make a blessing with him and come out to him. Then you will be able to eat, a man of his vine and a man of his fig tree, and drink, a man from the waters of his well]

Here, **a blessing**, meaning a gift, represents “a peace agreement,” since in this culture people exchanged gifts when they made peace agreements. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Make a peace agreement with me]

Quote: וְ⁠אִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵנָת֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵי־בוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
Note: Rabshakeh is using **a man of his** vine and **a man of his** fig tree as a common expression of the culture to mean “each man  may access his own.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and let each of you eat from his vine and fig tree]

Quote: עַד־בֹּאִ֕⁠י וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֥י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּ⁠אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֑ם אֶ֤רֶץ דָּגָן֙ וְ⁠תִיר֔וֹשׁ אֶ֥רֶץ לֶ֖חֶם וּ⁠כְרָמִֽים
Note: There are three levels of quotation here. Isaiah is quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. The Rabshakeh is quoting the king of Assyria (level 2), also continuing from the previous verse. The king is quoting Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

Quote: עַד־בֹּאִ֕⁠י וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֥י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּ⁠אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֑ם אֶ֤רֶץ דָּגָן֙ וְ⁠תִיר֔וֹשׁ אֶ֥רֶץ לֶ֖חֶם וּ⁠כְרָמִֽים
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. # Introduction to Isaiah 37

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the story that begins in chapter 36.

  1. Hezekiah sends his officials to Isaiah (1–4)
  2. Yahweh promises through Isaiah that he will rescue Jerusalem (5–7)
  3. The Rabshakeh leaves, but the Assyrian king sends more messengers (8–13)
  4. Hezekiah prays to Yahweh for deliverance (14–20)
  5. Yahweh responds to Hezekiah through Isaiah (21–35)
  6. The army of Assyria is destroyed and its king is murdered (36–38)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Sennacherib’s sons kill him?

The story records in 37:38 that after Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, while he was worshiping in the temple of the Assyrian god Nisroch, Adrammelech and Sharezer, two of his sons, assassinated him. They did that because of a bitter conflict over who would succeed him as king, as ancient Assyrian sources report. The crown prince Assur-nadin-shumi died, and Sennacherib at first named Adrammelech his heir. But later he replaced him with Esarhaddon, a younger son, for reasons that the sources do not specify. This made Adrammelech very angry, but Sennacherib refused to reinstate him. So he conspired with his brother Sharezer to assassinate their father. They had hoped to seize power for themselves, but they had to flee, and Esarhaddon became the next king.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Levels of quotation

As in chapter 36, there are two long quotations in this chapter that contain multiple levels of quotation. They are in verses 10–13 and 21–35. Notes describe ways of indicating the speakers throughout these quotations. See what you did in the case of the quotations in the previous chapter, and present these quotations in the same way.

### Images in the king of Assyria’s boast

In verse 24, Yahweh uses vivid imagery to depict how the Assyrian king has been boasting of his military conquests. Here is an explanation of the various images that he uses.
- As Yahweh quotes him, Assyrian king is speaking as if he had actually gone up the highest and most remote mountains of **Lebanon** and cut down its tallest and most valuable trees.
- He is using **Lebanon** to represent the entire geographical area of which Israel is a part.
- He is using the giant **trees** that grow in Lebanon to represent huge, strong entities, so that his boast to have cut them down means that he has defeated powerful foes.
- By **the lodging place of its end**, he means the place where his army would stop at the end of a successful campaign to conquer the whole country, that is, Jerusalem.
- By **the forest of its garden** (that is, its forest that is like a garden), he means the place where the forest has been most transformed by cultivation into a park for human recreation and enjoyment. This seems to represent the grounds of the royal palace and temple, particularly in light of how extensively cedar and cypress wood was used in the construction of those buildings.
Consider how best to represent these images in your translation. A note to this verse suggests one possible way to do that.
