Quote: הַ⁠הִצִּ֨ילוּ אוֹתָ֜⁠ם אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִשְׁחִ֣יתוּ אֲבוֹתַ֔⁠י אֶת־גּוֹזָ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־חָרָ֑ן וְ⁠רֶ֥צֶף וּ⁠בְנֵי־עֶ֖דֶן אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּ⁠תְלַשָּֽׂר
Note: The Assyrian king is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The gods of the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan and Haran and Rezeph and the sons of Eden who were in Tel Assar, did not deliver any of them!]

Quote: הַ⁠הִצִּ֨ילוּ אוֹתָ֜⁠ם אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִשְׁחִ֣יתוּ אֲבוֹתַ֔⁠י אֶת־גּוֹזָ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־חָרָ֑ן וְ⁠רֶ֥צֶף וּ⁠בְנֵי־עֶ֖דֶן אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּ⁠תְלַשָּֽׂר
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Remind Hezekiah that the gods of the nations that my fathers destroyed did not deliver them, Gozan and Haran and Rezeph and the sons of Eden who were in Tel Assar.]
The Assyrian king is using the word **fathers** to mean his ancestors. Alternate translation: [my ancestors]
The expression **sons of Eden** refers to the people who lived in the region of Eden. Alternate translation: [the Edenites]

Quote: אַיֵּ֤ה מֶֽלֶךְ־חֲמָת֙ וּ⁠מֶ֣לֶךְ אַרְפָּ֔ד וּ⁠מֶ֖לֶךְ לָעִ֣יר סְפַרְוָ֑יִם הֵנַ֖ע וְ⁠עִוָּֽה
Note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The kings of Hamath and Arpad and of the cities of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah are all gone!]

Quote: אַיֵּ֤ה מֶֽלֶךְ־חֲמָת֙ וּ⁠מֶ֣לֶךְ אַרְפָּ֔ד וּ⁠מֶ֖לֶךְ לָעִ֣יר סְפַרְוָ֑יִם הֵנַ֖ע וְ⁠עִוָּֽה
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Remind Hezekiah that Assyrians defeated the kings of Hamath and Arpad and of the cities of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah, so all those kings no longer rule.]

In this expression, the words **king** and **city** are singular in form, but they refers to the kings of all three of the cities listed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. Alternate translation: [or the kings of the cities of Sepharvaim, Hena, or Ivvah]

Quote: וַ⁠יִּקַּ֨ח חִזְקִיָּ֧הוּ אֶת־הַ⁠סְּפָרִ֛ים מִ⁠יַּ֥ד הַ⁠מַּלְאָכִ֖ים וַ⁠יִּקְרָאֵ֑⁠הוּ
Note: While the term **writings** is plural, the author’s use of the singular pronoun **it** in the next clause and the next sentence shows that Hezekiah received one letter from the king of Assyria. (His messengers apparently read the contents of this letter out loud to Hezekiah and then gave him the written copy of the message for confirmation.) So in this context, the term **writings** has the sense of “the things that the king had written.” You could indicate that explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. You could also use singular forms instead of plural ones. Alternate translation: [Then the messengers handed Hezekiah a written copy of what they had said, and he read the things that the king had written] or [Then Hezekiah took the letter from the hand of the messengers, and he read it]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, Isaiah is marking travel for change in elevation, **up**. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And he went]

When Hezekiah **spread** the letter **out** (unrolled the scroll on which it was written) so that the contents were visible to Yahweh, this was a symbolic action by which he was asking for help by calling Yahweh’s attention to what Sennacherib had written, specifically the claim that Yahweh was no different from the gods of other nations. (Hezekiah did not believe that Yahweh would not know what was in the letter if he did not unroll the scroll. Also, Sennacherib’s messengers had stated the contents out loud before giving him this written version.) If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and Hezekiah spread it out before Yahweh as an appeal for help]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of Yahweh] or [where Yahweh could see it]

Here, **saying** represents the words of Hezekiah’s prayer that follow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Hezekiah prayed to Yahweh with these words]
See how you decided to represent the phrase **saying** when it introduces a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [and he said]

Hezekiah is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **made** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that God alone was the maker of **the heavens and the earth**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You, only you, made the heavens and the earth]

Hezekiah is speaking as if he wants Yahweh physically to **Incline** his **ear**, that is, to lean over the way someone would do to listen closely to someone who was located below him, such as a supplicant who was kneeling in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully]

Quote: הַטֵּ֨ה יְהוָ֤ה אָזְנְ⁠ךָ֙ וּֽ⁠שְׁמָ֔ע פְּקַ֧ח יְהוָ֛ה עֵינֶ֖⁠ךָ וּ⁠רְאֵ֑ה וּ⁠שְׁמַ֗ע
Note: The phrases **Incline your ear**, **hear**,  **Open  your eyes**, **see**, and **hear** an imperatives, but they communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please incline your ear, Yahweh, and hear. Please open your eyes, Yahweh, and see. And please hear]

In this verse, the word **land** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the lands of these **nations** as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “land.” Alternate translation: [and their lands]

Quote: וְ⁠נָתֹ֥ן אֶת־אֱלֹהֵי⁠הֶ֖ם בָּ⁠אֵ֑שׁ כִּי֩ לֹ֨א אֱלֹהִ֜ים הֵ֗מָּה כִּ֣י אִם־מַעֲשֵׂ֧ה יְדֵֽי־אָדָ֛ם עֵ֥ץ וָ⁠אֶ֖בֶן וַֽ⁠יְאַבְּדֽוּ⁠ם
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since their gods are not gods, but rather the work of the hands of man, wood and stone, they have put them in the fire and destroyed them]

Hezekiah is using one part of people, their **hands**, to mean all of them in the act of making **gods** out of **wood** and **stone**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the work of craftsmen]
See how you translated the similar expression in [5:3](../05/03.md) and [5:5](../05/05.md).

Here, **hand** represents the power/control/capability of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from his power]

Quote: לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁר֙ הִתְפַּלַּ֣לְתָּ אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־סַנְחֵרִ֖יב מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
Note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the long quotation in verses 21–35, in which there are multiple levels of quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this verse so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling him that Yahweh, the God of Israel, said that he had heard what he had prayed to him about Sennacherib, the king of Assyria]

Quote: זֶ֣ה הַ⁠דָּבָ֔ר אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה עָלָ֑י⁠ו בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [This is the word that Yahweh has spoken about him. He says that the virgin, the daughter of Zion, despises him, she derides him. The daughter of Jerusalem shakes a head after him]

Quote: בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: Isaiah is speaking as if the city of **Jerusalem** were actually a mother and its inhabitants were her **daughter**. (In the first instance of this image, he uses the term **Zion**, the mountain on which the city was located, to represent the city itself.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Jerusalem despise you, they deride you. The people of Jerusalem shake their heads after you]

Quote: בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: Isaiah is using the present tense to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to show that it will certainly happen and that it will happen soon. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense. Alternate translation: [The people of Jerusalem will despise you, they will deride you. The people of Jerusalem will shake their heads after you]

Quote: בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: Yahweh, speaking through Isaiah, is speaking to someone whom he knows cannot hear him, the king of Assyria. He is doing this to communicate to Hezekiah that he feels very strongly about that king’s arrogance and mockery. If it would be helpful in your language, here and through verse 28, you could translate these words as if Yahweh were speaking directly to Hezekiah about the king of Assyria. Alternate translation: [The virgin, the daughter of Zion, despises him, she derides him. The daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head after him] or [The people of Jerusalem will despise him, they will deride him. The people of Jerusalem will shake their heads after him]

In this culture, shaking or wagging one’s head at a person was a symbolic action by which people showed contempt and expressed mockery toward that person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [The daughter will shake her head disdainfully and mockingly after you]

Isaiah assumes that his listeners will know that by **after you**, he means that the Assyrians will flee from Jerusalem and that the people of the city will make this gesture at them as they run away. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at you as you flee] or [at him as he flees]

Quote: אֶת־מִ֤י חֵרַ֨פְתָּ֙ וְ⁠גִדַּ֔פְתָּ וְ⁠עַל־מִ֖י הֲרִימ֣וֹתָה קּ֑וֹל וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֥א מָר֛וֹם עֵינֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֶל־קְד֥וֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh asks Sennacherib whom he has mocked and taunted. Yahweh asks him against whom he has raised a voice and lifted his eyes upward. The answer is that Sennacherib has done that against him, the Holy One of Israel!]

Quote: אֶת־מִ֤י חֵרַ֨פְתָּ֙ וְ⁠גִדַּ֔פְתָּ וְ⁠עַל־מִ֖י הֲרִימ֣וֹתָה קּ֑וֹל וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֥א מָר֛וֹם עֵינֶ֖י⁠ךָ
Note: Yahweh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You must realize whom have you mocked and taunted! You must realize against whom have you raised a voice and lifted your eyes upward!]

The action of **lifting** his **eyes upward** was a symbolic action by which the king of Assyria showed arrogance and defiance toward Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and arrogantly lifted your eyes upward] or [and defiantly lifted your eyes upward]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to describe the holy God with whom the Israelites are in a covenant relationship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the holy God with whom you Israelites are in a covenant relationship]

Quote: בְּ⁠יַ֣ד עֲבָדֶי⁠ךָ֮ חֵרַ֣פְתָּ ׀ אֲדֹנָ⁠י֒ וַ⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְחַ֣ר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָבוֹא֙ מְר֣וֹם קִצּ֔⁠וֹ יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
Note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Isaiah told Hezekiah in his message (level 1), continuing from the previous verses. This includes what, according to Isaiah, Yahweh was saying to Hezekiah, also continuing from the previous verse (level 2). This includes a quotation from the king of Assyria (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

Quote: בְּ⁠יַ֣ד עֲבָדֶי⁠ךָ֮ חֵרַ֣פְתָּ ׀ אֲדֹנָ⁠י֒ וַ⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְחַ֣ר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָבוֹא֙ מְר֣וֹם קִצּ֔⁠וֹ יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that by the hand of his servants he mocked him and said boastfully that with the multitude of his chariotry, he went up to the height of the mountains, the recesses of Lebanon. He boasted that he cut down the heights of its cedars, the choicest of its cypress trees, that he might enter the height of its end, the forest of its orchard]

Quote: בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְחַ֣ר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָבוֹא֙ מְר֣וֹם קִצּ֔⁠וֹ יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
Note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the elaborate comparison that the Assyrian king is drawing in this verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I commanded my chariot forces and invaded this land, even though it was remote from me and secure. I defeated the most powerful and skillful opponents. Now I am going to enter Jerusalem and capture the royal palace and temple]
Isaiah uses the word **servants** to mean the agency or authority of the servants. Alternate translation: [Through the agency of your servants]

The Assyrian king is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I went up** already includes this meaning. He is doing that for emphasis because he is boasting. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and said boastfully, “With the multitude of my chariotry, I myself went up]

Quote: אֲנִ֥י קַ֖רְתִּי וְ⁠שָׁתִ֣יתִי מָ֑יִם וְ⁠אַחְרִב֙ בְּ⁠כַף־פְּעָמַ֔⁠י כֹּ֖ל יְאֹרֵ֥י מָצֽוֹר
Note: This verse is the conclusion of the third-level quotation that begins in the previous verse. If you have decided to use punctuation to mark levels of quotation, end this verse with the appropriate punctuation for closing a third-level quotation.

Quote: אֲנִ֥י קַ֖רְתִּי וְ⁠שָׁתִ֣יתִי מָ֑יִם וְ⁠אַחְרִב֙ בְּ⁠כַף־פְּעָמַ֔⁠י כֹּ֖ל יְאֹרֵ֥י מָצֽוֹר
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that the Assyrian king has boasted that he has dug wells and drunk waters. He has also boasted that he will dry up all of the streams of Matsor with the sole of his feet]

The Assyrian king is stating the pronoun **I** explicitly, even though the verb translated as **I dug** already includes this meaning, because he is boasting. See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [I myself dug, and I drank the waters]

The Assyrian king could be saying: (1) that he was able to dig wells and drink water from them in foreign countries. This would be a boast that his armies could successfully traverse arid, desolate areas. Alternate translation: [I have dug wells and drunk water from them] or (2) that he was able to dig wells and find water in places where no one suspected it would be. This might be a taunt at Hezekiah, who, according to [2 Chronicles 32:3–4](../2ch/32/03.md), tried to eliminate the supply of water around the city of Jerusalem to thwart the Assyrians. Alternate translation: [I have been able to dig wells and find water in places my enemies did not expect]

The word **Matsor** is another name for Egypt. (The word is related to the word for “border.” Egypt was considered the border of Israel.) Alternate translation: [And with the sole of my feet I will dry up all of the streams of Egypt]

In this verse, the word **sole** is singular in form, but the king is using it to refer to both of his feet. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural or dual form of “sole.” Alternate translation: [And with the soles of my feet I will dry up all of the streams of Egypt]

The king is speaking as if he could actually **dry up all the streams of** Egypt with the soles of his **feet**, the way a person could stamp out a small puddle. The **streams** of Egypt, meaning the Nile and its tributary, represent something formidable, like the giant trees of Lebanon in the previous verse. The king is boasting that after conquering Jerusalem, he will conquer the Egyptian empire without great effort. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And next I will conquer Egypt without great effort]

Quote: הֲ⁠לֽוֹא־שָׁמַ֤עְתָּ לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אוֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ עַתָּ֣ה הֲבֵאתִ֔י⁠הָ וּ⁠תְהִ֗י לְ⁠הַשְׁא֛וֹת גַּלִּ֥ים נִצִּ֖ים עָרִ֥ים בְּצֻרֽוֹת
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that the Assyrian king must surely have heard that from long ago, he did it; that from days of antiquity, he formed it. Now Yahweh has brought it, that the king should be for devastating fortified cities into ruined heaps]

Quote: הֲ⁠לֽוֹא־שָׁמַ֤עְתָּ לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אוֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ
Note: Yahweh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely you must have heard that from long ago, I did it; that from days of antiquity, I formed it]

Quote: לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אוֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ
Note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I decided a long time ago that this would happen]
Yahweh is using the term **days of antiquity** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from ancient times]

The expression **ruined** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [into heaps of ruins]

Quote: וְ⁠יֹֽשְׁבֵי⁠הֶן֙ קִצְרֵי־יָ֔ד חַ֖תּוּ וָ⁠בֹ֑שׁוּ הָי֞וּ עֵ֤שֶׂב שָׂדֶה֙ וִ֣⁠ירַק דֶּ֔שֶׁא חֲצִ֣יר גַּגּ֔וֹת וּ⁠שְׁדֵמָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י קָמָֽה
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that their dwellers are short of hand, they feel dismay and feel shame. They are vegetation of the field or green of herb; grass of roofs, blasting to the face of growing up]

Yahweh is using **short of hand** as a common expression of this culture to mean “powerless.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are powerless]

Quote: הָי֞וּ עֵ֤שֶׂב שָׂדֶה֙ וִ֣⁠ירַק דֶּ֔שֶׁא חֲצִ֣יר גַּגּ֔וֹת וּ⁠שְׁדֵמָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י קָמָֽה
Note: Yahweh is speaking as if the people whom the Assyrians are conquering are actually tender plants that are defenseless against certain threats. Plants growing in the **field** can be easily trampled, for example, while **grass** growing on the flat **roofs** of this culture could easily wither in the heat of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They are as defenseless before the Assyrians as vegetation or green herbs out in the field or as grass on a flat roof, which withers in the heat of the sun]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe an **herb** that is characterized by being **green**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or green herbs]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [grass on roofs, which the sun blasts before it can grow up]

Quote: וְ⁠שִׁבְתְּ⁠ךָ֛ וְ⁠צֵאתְ⁠ךָ֥ וּ⁠בוֹאֲ⁠ךָ֖ יָדָ֑עְתִּי וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הִֽתְרַגֶּזְ⁠ךָ֥ אֵלָֽ⁠י
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh says he knows the dwelling of the king of Assyria and his going out and his coming in and his raging against him]

Quote: וְ⁠שִׁבְתְּ⁠ךָ֛ וְ⁠צֵאתְ⁠ךָ֥ וּ⁠בוֹאֲ⁠ךָ֖ יָדָ֑עְתִּי וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הִֽתְרַגֶּזְ⁠ךָ֥ אֵלָֽ⁠י
Note: Yahweh is using two different conditions, either being at home or leaving or returning, to represent all conditions that the king of Assyria might be in. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [But I know everything about you, including how you rage against me]

The second-level quotation that begins in verse 21, in which Yahweh addresses the king of Assyria even though he cannot hear him, ends with this verse. If you have decided to use punctuation to mark levels of quotation, end this verse with the appropriate punctuation for closing a second-level quotation.

If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that because of his raging against him and because his arrogance has come up into his ears, Yahweh will put his hook in the king’s nose and his bit in the king’s lips. And he will make him return on the way by which he came]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and because your arrogance has come up into my ears]

Here, **ears** represent hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and your arrogance has come up into my hearing] or [and I have heard from heaven the arrogant things you have been saying]

Yahweh is speaking as if he were actually going to put a **hook** in the **nose** of the king of Assyria and a **bit** in his **lips**, as if the king were an animal such as people would control by these means. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will control you by powerful means, and I will make you return on the way by which you came]
Here, the king’s **lips** represent his mouth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your mouth]

Isaiah is now addressing Hezekiah directly. He is no longer speaking in the first person on behalf of Yahweh (although he will do that again in verses 32–34). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And this will be the sign for you, Hezekiah]

If your language would not represent number in forms such as **second** or **third**, you could represent these numbers in forms that your language would use. Alternate translation: [and in year two , its offspring. But in year three] or [and next year, its offspring. But in the year after that]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [you will eat its offspring] or [you will eat what grows from that]

Quote: וְ⁠יָ֨סְפָ֜ה פְּלֵיטַ֧ת בֵּית־יְהוּדָ֛ה הַ⁠נִּשְׁאָרָ֖ה שֹׁ֣רֶשׁ לְ⁠מָ֑טָּה וְ⁠עָשָׂ֥ה פְרִ֖י לְ⁠מָֽעְלָ⁠ה
Note: Isaiah is speaking as if the Judeans were actually a plant that would **{take} root** and **make fruit**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the Judeans who have survived and remain will establish themselves in their land again and have many children]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **survival**, you could express the same idea in another way, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [And the remaining survivors of the house of Judah]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Judah** figuratively means all the people descended from Judah, one of the sons of Israel. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Judah]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and survivors will come out from Mount Zion]

Some ancient manuscripts read “The zeal of Yahweh of armies will do this.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “The zeal of Yahweh will do this.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Isaiah is speaking of the **zeal** of Yahweh as if it were a living thing that could do the things he describes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will do this in his zeal] or [Yahweh will zealously do this]

Quote: לָ⁠כֵ֗ן כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר לֹ֤א יָבוֹא֙ אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את וְ⁠לֹֽא־יוֹרֶ֥ה שָׁ֖ם חֵ֑ץ וְ⁠לֹֽא־יְקַדְּמֶ֣⁠נָּה מָגֵ֔ן וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִשְׁפֹּ֥ךְ עֳלֶ֖י⁠הָ סֹלְלָֽה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Therefore Yahweh says about the king of Assyria that he will not come to this city, and he will not shoot an arrow there, and he will not come before it with a shield, and he will not pour out a mound against it]

Quote: בַּ⁠דֶּ֥רֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֖א בָּ֣⁠הּ יָשׁ֑וּב וְ⁠אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּ֛את לֹ֥א יָב֖וֹא נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh declares that the king of Assyria will return by the way on which he came, and he will not come to this city]

Quote: בַּ⁠דֶּ֥רֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֖א בָּ֣⁠הּ יָשׁ֑וּב וְ⁠אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּ֛את לֹ֥א יָב֖וֹא
Note: Yahweh is describing one event before describing another event that would precede it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [He will not come to this city, but he will return by the way on which he came]

Quote: וְ⁠גַנּוֹתִ֛י עַל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּ֖את לְ⁠הֽוֹשִׁיעָ֑⁠הּ לְמַֽעֲנִ֔⁠י וּ⁠לְמַ֖עַן דָּוִ֥ד עַבְדִּֽ⁠י
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that he will cover over this city to save it, for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant]

Yahweh is speaking as if he were actually going to **cover over** the city of Jerusalem to protect it, as with a shield. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for I will protect this city]
Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [this will happen because]

This verse ends the long first-level quotation that begins at verse 20. It also contains a second-level quotation from Yahweh that concludes at the end of the verse. If you have decided to use punctuation to mark levels of quotation, end this verse with the appropriate punctuation for closing both a second-level and first-level quotation.

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [killing 185,000 soldiers]

The pronoun **they** refers to the soldiers in the Assyrian camp whom the angel of Yahweh did not kill. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the surviving soldiers arose early]

Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [they saw that]

Quote: וַ⁠יִּסַּ֣ע וַ⁠יֵּ֔לֶךְ וַ⁠יָּ֖שָׁב סַנְחֵרִ֣יב מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֑וּר וַ⁠יֵּ֖שֶׁב בְּ⁠נִֽינְוֵֽה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could name the king in the earlier part of the sentence and use the pronoun in the later part of the sentence. Alternate translation: [And Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, departed and went, and he returned and stayed in Nineveh]

The author is using the phrase **And it happened** to introduce a new development within the event of the Assyrians invading Judah. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new development, as modeled by the UST.

Some ancient manuscripts read “and Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him with the sword.” Other ancient manuscripts read “and Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword.” The ULT follows the reading that includes “his sons.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

The word **and** here indicates a contrast. The sons killed Sennacherib, **and they** themselves **escaped**. If it would be clearer in your language, you can indicate this contrast explicitly. Alternate translation: [and for their part, they escaped]

# Introduction to Isaiah 38

## Structure and Formatting

  1. Yahweh heals Hezekiah of a deadly illness (1–8)
  2. A song of thanksgiving that Hezekiah wrote (9–20)
  3. Details of how Yahweh healed Hezekiah (21–22)

The phrase **In those days** is a way of referring to the time period being described. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [At around that time]

Quote: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ צַ֣ו לְ⁠בֵיתֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֛י מֵ֥ת אַתָּ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִֽחְיֶֽה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that you should command regarding your house, for you are dying, and you will not live]

Quote: צַ֣ו לְ⁠בֵיתֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֛י מֵ֥ת אַתָּ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִֽחְיֶֽה
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since you are dying, and you will not live, command regarding your house]

Here Hezekiah’s **house** could represent: (1) his household affairs. Alternate translation: [Put your affairs in order] or (2) his royal dynasty. Hezekiah lived 15 years after this illness, but his son and successor Manasseh was 12 years old when he became king, indicating that Hezekiah did not have an heir at this time. He would therefore have had to identify someone as his successor. Alternate translation: [Name your successor]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [you will surely die from this illness]

Hezekiah is not suggesting that Yahweh does not **remember** these things and needs to be reminded of them. He is asking Yahweh to take them into consideration. Alternate translation: [consider] or [take into consideration]

Here **walked** is a metaphor for how Hezekiah has conducted his life before Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have lived]

The phrase **to your face** is a way of saying in your presence or under your authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [faithfully]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s intentions and commitments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in complete devotion]

The phrase ** good in your eyes** means what you consider to be good or what you approve of. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I have done what you consider to be good]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And Hezekiah wept bitterly]

The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Yahweh spoke a message to Isaiah. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in [1 Samuel 15:10](rc://*/tn/help/1sa/15/10). Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke a message to Isaiah]

Quote: הָל֞וֹךְ וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ דָּוִ֣ד אָבִ֔י⁠ךָ שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ אֶת־תְּפִלָּתֶ֔⁠ךָ רָאִ֖יתִי אֶת־דִּמְעָתֶ֑⁠ךָ הִנְ⁠נִי֙ יוֹסִ֣ף עַל־יָמֶ֔י⁠ךָ חֲמֵ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָֽה
Note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Yahweh said (level 1). Yahweh is quoting what he wants Isaiah to say to Hezekiah. (level 2). This includes a quotation from Yahweh himself. (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation, in this verse and at the end of the next verse. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

Quote: הָל֞וֹךְ וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ דָּוִ֣ד אָבִ֔י⁠ךָ שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ אֶת־תְּפִלָּתֶ֔⁠ךָ רָאִ֖יתִי אֶת־דִּמְעָתֶ֑⁠ךָ הִנְ⁠נִי֙ יוֹסִ֣ף עַל־יָמֶ֔י⁠ךָ חֲמֵ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָֽה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Go and tell Hezekiah that I, Yahweh, the God of David his father, have heard his prayer and have seen his weeping. I am going to add fifteen years to his life]

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making a solemn declaration. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [I say]

Yahweh refers to David as Hezekiah’s **father**, though David was actually his ancestor several generations back. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your ancestor]

Quote: הִנְ⁠נִי֙ יוֹסִ֣ף עַל־יָמֶ֔י⁠ךָ חֲמֵ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָֽה
Note: Yahweh is using a common expression of this culture, **Behold me**, to indicate that he is about to do something. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in [37:7](../37/07.md). Alternate translation: [I am going to heal you]

Quote: וּ⁠מִ⁠כַּ֤ף מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ אַצִּ֣ילְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֑את וְ⁠גַנּוֹתִ֖י עַל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּֽאת
Note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be quotations within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah that I say that I will deliver him and this city from the palm of the king of Assyria, and I will cover over this city]

Quote: וּ⁠מִ⁠כַּ֤ף מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ אַצִּ֣ילְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֑את
Note: Here, **palm** represents the power or control of the king of Assyria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will deliver you and this city from the power of the king of Assyria]
See how you translated the similar expression in [37:35](../37/35.md). Alternate translation: [And I will protect this city]

Yahweh is using a common expression of this culture, **Behold me**, to indicate that he is about to do something. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in [37:7](../37/07.md). Alternate translation: [I am going to make the shadow return on the stairs]

The phrase **the stairs of Ahaz** describes a structure that King Ahaz, the father of Hezekiah, built to track the passage of time. It showed the time of day by the position of the shadow that a pole cast on a series of **steps** below the pole. Such a structure is sometimes called a “shadow clock.” It is similar to what many cultures know as a sundial. If your readers would not be familiar with such a structure, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [on the steps of the shadow clock that King Ahaz had built] or [on the sundial of King Ahaz]

Quote: מִכְתָּ֖ב לְ⁠חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה בַּ⁠חֲלֹת֕⁠וֹ וַ⁠יְחִ֖י מֵ⁠חָלְיֽ⁠וֹ
Note: What follows in verses 10-20 is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

Hezekiah is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is the person making the statement. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I, Hezekiah, said]

Hezekiah is using **In the quiet of my days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the prime of my life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In the prime of my life]

Here Hezekiah is speaking as if **Sheol**, the place of the dead, were a walled city that he would enter through its **gates**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will go to Sheol when I die]

Hezekiah is using the possessive form to describe **gates** that are characterized by belonging to **Sheol**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into the gates that lead to Sheol]

The expression **I am visited** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is taking from me]

The implication is that Yahweh is the one who has cut Hezekiah’s life short. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I am being punished by Yahweh]

Hezekiah is using **I will not see Yah** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will no longer experience Yahweh’s presence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will not be in the presence of Yah]

# Introduction to Part Seven of the Book of Isaiah

Part Seven of the book of Isaiah (chapters 40–55) addresses the community of Judean exiles in Babylon. It encourages them to believe that, as incredible as this might seem, King Cyrus of Persia will defeat the Babylonians and take over their empire, and he will allow exiled peoples to return to their homelands. It challenges them to stop worshiping Babylonian gods and to start worshiping Yahweh again.

See the discussion in the introduction to the book of Isaiah of how, in the view of some interpreters, the oracles in this part of the book appear to have been spoken by a living member of the Judean exile community in Babylon. Other interpreters, as that discussion also indicates, believe that Isaiah son of Amoz spoke all of the words in the book that bears his name, 150 years before the end of the exile. Both of these positions are held and defended by scholars who are equally committed to the inspiration and authority of the Bible as the word of God and to God’s ability to reveal future events to his prophets. It is not necessary to decide between these positions in order to translate this book. These notes use the name Isaiah conventionally throughout to mean the author or authors of the book of Isaiah.

In this part of the book, the prophet speaks many times about a special servant whom Yahweh has appointed to accomplish his purposes in the world. In some contexts, this servant is clearly King Cyrus. In other contexts, the servant is identified as the nation of Israel. In still other contexts, it seems to be the prophet himself. And in some places, the servant is an unnamed person who will appear sometime in the future. From the character and actions of this person, Christian interpreters have long recognized these places as prophecies about Jesus the Messiah.

This part of the book has two major sections. In the first section (chapters 40–48), in a sustained series of oracles, the prophet presents an expansive vision of the magnificent possibilities that lie before the Judean exiles if they will only return to Yahweh and trust in his promises. This section, like others in the book, is built out of individual oracles that are connected by similarities in language and imagery. Over the course of these oracles, the prophet proclaims to his fellow Judean exiles in Babylon that Yahweh wants to bring them back to their land so that they can be a messenger to all nations. He describes how Yahweh wants to use the Persian emperor Cyrus as the instrument of this deliverance. And he pleads with the people to trust in Yahweh, to believe that he hasn’t abandoned them and that he is able to rescue them.

In the second section (chapters 49–55), the prophet speaks very personally, telling his own story. He describes how the people have rejected his message and even attacked him for proclaiming it. Nevertheless, he finds renewed strength and confidence when the Lord affirms his prophetic mission and shows him that it will ultimately have more far-reaching effects than he has yet imagined. The oracles in this section are also the ones that speak most prophetically and poignantly about the future work of Jesus.

# Introduction to Isaiah 41

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter consists of a single poetic oracle that has several parts. It describes a court proceeding between Yahweh and the idols of the nations. The Judean exiles were tempted to depend on those idols because they believed that their own God had either abandoned them or could do nothing to help them.  In this oracle, Yahweh reclaims the loyalty of those who should be trusting him. He demonstrates that the gods that idols represent do not exist, while he alone has the knowledge to declare what will happen and the power to make it happen.

  1. Yahweh summons the nations to court (1)
  2. Yahweh is the true God because only he predicted what is now happening (2–4)
  3. The nations join together to make idols they hope will deliver them (5–7)
  4. Yahweh encourages the Israelites not to fear (8–20)
  5. Yahweh challenges the idols to respond, but they say and do nothing (21–24)
  6. Yahweh makes his closing argument (25–29)

# Introduction to Isaiah 44

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents several oracles that continue to develop the themes of this part of the book.

  1. People will once again be proud to be Israelites when Yahweh restores them (1–5)
  2. Yahweh is the only true God; idols are human fabrications (6–23)
  3. Yahweh is all-powerful and all-knowing, and he will make Cyrus successful (24–28)

The first oracle in this chapter (verses 1–5) is a response to the preceding one (43:22–28). That oracle describes how it has become shameful to be an Israelite. In this oracle, Yahweh promises that he will restore and bless the Israelites so that it will once again be an honor to be one of them.

The third oracle (verses 24–28) introduces Cyrus by name for the first time as the person Yahweh has chosen to accomplish his purpose of bringing the exiles back to their land.

# Introduction to Isaiah 46

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents a single oracle that continues to develop the themes of this part of the book.

  1. The Babylonians will carry away their idols in disgrace when Cyrus defeats them (1–13)

This oracle emphasizes that Yahweh alone knows and declares the future, while idols are simply something that people make. The gods they represent are nonexistent and worthless. Yahweh has always had good plans for the people of Israel, and he will fulfill them.

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Bel and Nebo both bow low]
The words **Bel** and **Nebo** are the names of Babylonian gods.

The implication is that the images of these gods are being loaded onto the pack animals to be carried away into captivity. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [their images are loaded onto animals and beasts]

# Introduction to Isaiah 49

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the second section of Part Seven of the book of Isaiah.  The prophet now speaks very personally, telling his own story, as he describes how the people have rejected his message and even attacked him for proclaiming it. Nevertheless, he finds renewed strength and confidence when Yahweh affirms his prophetic mission and shows him that it will ultimately have even more far-reaching effects than he has yet imagined.

This chapter presents four oracles that begin to develop these themes.

  1. Yahweh has prepared the prophet from birth, and his message will reach all nations (1–6)
  2. Yahweh will use the prophet to help rescue the Israelites from exile (7–13)
  3. Yahweh has not forsaken the Israelites; he will abundantly restore their exiles (14–23)
  4. Yahweh will defeat the Israelites’ enemies and claim the Israelites as his prize (24–26)

# Introduction to Isaiah 50

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents two oracles that continue to develop the themes of this part of the book.

  1. The Israelites are suffering because they disobeyed Yahweh (1–3)
  2. The prophet challenges the people who have been mistreating him (4–11)

The second oracle provides a fascinating glimpse into the prophet’s life. He relates how God wakes him up each morning and has him listen to his word for that day. He also describes the physical abuse he has suffered for delivering these messages: beatings on his back (perhaps some kind of community-sanctioned punishment) and the plucking out of his beard (both a painful torture and a degrading insult in this culture). It appears that the Israelites have settled into the belief that God has abandoned them. Because the prophet has had the audacity to challenge their complacent assumptions and is claiming that God wants to rescue them, they are accusing him of misrepresenting God and being a false prophet. This oracle is an answer to those accusations. The prophet records how he has faithfully fulfilled God’s calling, and he challenges his opponents to prove otherwise. He appeals to all those in the community who are sympathetic to his message to trust in Yahweh. He warns that those who rely on themselves instead will suffer in the end.

# Introduction to Isaiah 51

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents three oracles that continue to develop the themes of this part of the book.

In the first oracle (verses 1–8), Yahweh encourages the Israelites who trust him to wait patiently and confidently for him to deliver them. This continues the themes of the last oracle in chapter 50.

The other two oracles in this chapter (verses 9–16 and 17–23) are part of a series of three oracles that each begin with a double call for someone to “awake.” (The third oracle is in 52:1–12). First the prophet calls upon the “arm of Yahweh” to “awake.” He asks Yahweh to use his power to rescue the Israelites from exile, just as the rescued them from slavery in Egypt. Yahweh reassures him that he will use him to help rescue the people. The prophet then calls to Jerusalem, “Awaken yourself!” He promises that the people of the city will recover from defeat and that Yahweh will defeat their enemies. 

  1. Yahweh will rescue the people who trust in him (1–8)
  2. The prophet can be assured that Yahweh will use his power to help the Israelites (9–16)
  3. The people of Jerusalem will recover from their defeat (17–23)

# Introduction to Isaiah 52

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues to develop the themes of this part of the book.

It begins with an oracle (verses 1–12) in which the prophet once again encourages the people of Jerusalem (addressing them as “Zion”) that Yahweh will use his power to free their exiles and return them. He calls on Zion to “Awake, awake.”

The rest of this chapter (verses 13–15) is the first part of an oracle that also includes all of chapter 53. See the introduction to chapter 53 for a discussion of that whole oracle.

  1. Yahweh will use his power to free Jerusalem’s exiles and return them home (1–12)

# Introduction to Isaiah 53

## Structure and Formatting

Earlier in this second section of Part Seven of the book of Isaiah, the prophet called out, “Awake, awake!” to the arm of Yahweh (51:9). Yahweh said in response that he would pull his arm out of his robe and rescue the people. In the oracle that comprises all of this chapter (and the end of the previous chapter), Yahweh shows the prophet the unexpected way in which he will ultimately do that. He gives the prophet a further glimpse of what the coming servant figure, the Messiah, will do in the more distant future. (The future figure is in view here; when the prophet is speaking of himself as the servant, he says “I,” but here he says “he,” and he refers to himself and the rest of the people as “us.”) The prophet sees how the Messiah will bring a great deliverance to the whole world, far transcending the political liberation that Cyrus will bring to captive populations. Perhaps in part because of his own experiences of suffering and rejection at the hands of the people, the prophet is able to recognize how God will allow this future servant to suffer on behalf of the people. He sees and describes how his painful experiences will become the means by which God brings about worldwide salvation.

The New Testament explains that Jesus fulfilled this prophecy and accomplished the purposes it describes when he died for us on the cross. In fact, the book of Acts records a conversation (Acts 8:26–39) in which an important official of a foreign kingdom asks one of Jesus’ followers, a man named Philip, to explain this prophecy. “Who is the prophet talking about,” he asks, “himself or someone else?” Beginning with this passage, Philip tells the official the good news about Jesus.

  1. What the servant does will amaze people (52:13–15)
  2. The servant will be humble and not seem important (53:1–3)
  3. The servant will accept the punishment that sinful people deserve (53:4–6)
  4. The servant will willingly suffer injustice (53:7–9)
  5. The servant will be honored and rewarded for what he does (53:10–12)

# Introduction to Isaiah 54

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter consists of a single poetic oracle. It presents two extended images that describe how God will forgive and rescue the people. It first uses the restoration of a marriage as a symbol of reconciliation. The Lord speaks to an unnamed woman, who is probably Zion, representing of the nation, since that city is then addressed directly. He tells her that while she is now alone and childless, soon he will take her back as his wife and she will have so many children she will have to make extra room for them. The oracle then envisions the city rebuilt with dazzling precious stones. This represents the splendor of the peace and justice that will prevail in the restored community. There are echoes here of the oracles in which Jerusalem and Zion were told to “awake,” but now, in light of the future servant’s reconciling work, the vision is even more splendid and expansive.

  1. Yahweh will restore the Israelites like a man who takes back his wife (1–10)
  2. Jerusalem will be splendid, as if it were built with precious stones (11–17)

# Introduction to Isaiah 55

## Structure and Formatting

Part Seven of the book of Isaiah ends with an oracle that makes a final exhortation to the people. Yahweh speaks first, calling on them to come to him and enjoy wonderful food freely, “without silver, and without price.” He doesn’t primarily mean actual food, although he has promised throughout this part of the book that he will provide for their needs. Rather, he wants them to hear, understand, and embrace his offer to renew his covenant with them so that they can be restored to their land and be a “witness to the peoples” there.

The prophet speaks next, calling on his fellow exiles one more time to “return to Yahweh” and receive his forgiveness. Finally, Yahweh speaks again, assuring the people that while they may not always understand what he is doing, his purposes will be accomplished as surely as the rain and snow water the ground and make the plants grow.

The oracle ends with a reprise of an image that has recurred throughout Part Seven, that of a highway through the desert that will allow the exiles to return home. Now, as the Israelites travel this route, the desert shrubs are transformed into hardwood trees that clap their hands in celebration. The mountains and hills burst into singing. This is the joy that Yahweh is inviting his people to experience in a restored relationship with him.

  1. Yahweh invites the people into a renewed relationship with him (1–5)
  2. The prophet urges the people to return to Yahweh (6–7)
  3. Yahweh promises to do what he has said and bring the people back home (8–13)

# Isaiah 56 Introduction
# Introduction to Part Eight of the Book of Isaiah

Part Eight of the book of Isaiah (chapters 56–66) speaks to a situation some years after the one that Part Seven addresses. God’s promises through the prophet have begun to be fulfilled. The Persian emperor Cyrus has conquered Babylon and allowed the Jewish exiles to return home and start rebuilding Jerusalem. However, much still needs to happen within the community of returned exiles before it can fulfill the rest of Yahweh’s promises by becoming a witness to all nations of his glory and love. The people are falling back into the same sins of idolatry, oppression, and injustice that led Yahweh to take them away from the land in the first place. Many are worshiping Yahweh once again, but only through outward forms, not from the depths of their hearts. And so a further prophetic word is needed to call the people who have returned to their land to return wholeheartedly to their covenant relationship with Yahweh. The prophet speaks that word in these final chapters of the book.

This section of the book begins with an oracle (in verses 1–8 of this chapter) that stresses how important it is for the returned exiles to keep Yahweh’s covenant. They must honor him both through religious observances such as keeping the Sabbath and by maintaining justice. It highlights this importance by addressing the situation of two groups among the returned exiles who, according to the law of Moses, should be excluded from full participation in the life of the community, and most notably from its worship. The first group is Israelites whose ancestors include foreigners. Because certain foreign nations refused to help the Israelites when they came out of Egypt as refugees, their descendants were excluded from the community. The second group is eunuchs. In order to oppose certain pagan practices, the law of Moses forbade anyone who became a eunuch from entering the sanctuary. The returned exiles who are eunuchs, however, were made so through castration in order to serve in the Babylonian court. The prophet declares that these exclusions will no longer apply. # Isaiah 58 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This poetic chapter is a divine speech. Yahweh rebukes the people’s empty [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/fast]] and redefines the fast he accepts—justice for the oppressed and care for the poor—then promises blessing for honoring the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sabbath]].

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### True fasting

To “afflict the soul” (verses 3 and 5) means to fast. Yahweh insists that the fast he accepts is not ritual self-denial but acts of justice and mercy toward the oppressed.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unintroduced speech

Yahweh speaks from verse 1 with no speech introduction, and rhetorical questions in verses 5 through 7 carry his argument.

# Isaiah 61 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This poem opens with an anointed speaker proclaiming good news, comfort, and freedom to the afflicted (verses 1–3), promises Zion’s people restoration and honor (verses 4–9), and closes with a song of rejoicing (verses 10–11).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The year of favor of Yahweh

This recalls Israel’s year of release, when captives were freed and debts canceled, picturing Yahweh’s coming deliverance of his people. See [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/favor]].

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

Garments repeatedly stand for inner states—ashes for grief, a “garment of praise” and “robe of righteousness” for restored joy.
